What day is meant by "that day"? The first verse of our
text-certainly very familiar to many of us from listening to
Brahms' Requiem-runs: "So you have sorrow now, but 1
will see you again and your hearts will rejoice, and no one
will take your joy from you." These words were spoken before
the event of Christ's passion, and the day of reunion which
Christ promises is Easter Day. But it is Easter Day in a quite
special context of meaning. The phrase "on that day" occurs
twice in our text and we must remember that this expression
held a very special and secret meaning for primitive Christ-
ianity. The expression was used without further elucidation
and its implication was "the day of the Lord"
, i.e. the day of
His return, the day on which this world would come to an
end and a new heaven and earth would spring into being;
the day on which would be fulfilled the promise: "Behold,
I make all things new!" And the meaning of Jesus' words is
that the "day" which spells an end to this world has through
Easter Day mysteriously become a present reality for
believers. The believer through his faith to some extent
anticipates the dawning of that "day" on which all things
will be made new. How is this possible? The "day" when all
creation will be renewed is anticipated by the Christian
believer who is himself regenerated in his personal being, as
Paul says: "Therefore if any one is in Christ, he is a new
creation; the old has passed away, behold, the new has
come" (2 Cor. 5: 17).
Hence the first thing which our text teaches us is this: to
be a Christian, to believe, means to have anticipated the
time span of this world, to stand already at the terminal
point of this age. For such a one true prayer is already a
reality. But the promise of the gift of prayer is preceded by
the promise of the gift of joy, of a joy "which no one will
take from us"
. This implies a joy which is no longer threat-
ened by the world, because the believer is as it were already
